source.title: Do LLMs Really Forget? Evaluating Unlearning with Knowledge Correlation and Confidence Awareness
source.authors: Rong-Zhe Wei; Pei-Zhi Niu; Hans Hao-Hsun Hsu; Rui-Han Wu; Hao-Teng Yin; Mohsen Ghassemi; Yi-Fan Li; Vamsi K. Potluru; Eli Chien; Kamalika Chaudhuri; Olgica Milenkovic; Pan Li

record.tranche_reason: Applies several unlearning methods and evaluates residual target-fact inferability through correlated supporting subgraphs, a different evaluation of whether unlearning leaves knowledge recoverable. It does not test the specific fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompt attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates inference from post-unlearning supporting subgraphs and compares that evaluation with instance-level UES. The UES (Ours) values are recorded below, with the corresponding UES (Inst.) shown as the table's reference. The paper also reports utility metrics, judge validation, and confidence calibration; those are not separate rows here because they do not directly measure the claim's recovery attacks. No explicit never-trained model comparison is reported.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well an external LLM judge (GPT-o4-mini) can infer a forgotten triple from related facts the unlearned model still affirms. It does not measure whether the model itself regains or outputs the target. That is residual inferability by a third party, a related but different construct from recovery under fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization or prompting. It is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of A–F.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that current methods and instance-level evaluation overestimate unlearning effectiveness, because correlated, sometimes low-confidence retained facts allow the target to be inferred. They call for evaluation that accounts for knowledge correlation and confidence. They also report that no method gives a good effectiveness–utility trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: Applies commonly used methods (GA, RL, NPO, NegGrad+, SCRUB) to relational facts using its own unlearning setup and evaluates them with correlated-subgraph inference. It does not reproduce the fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting recovery procedures in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model, unlearning format (sentence versus QA), method, and full-model versus LoRA tuning. QA-based unlearning often gives higher UES but the authors report utility costs; lowering the supporting-subgraph entropy threshold also increases UES.

fits_no_version.finding: After GA, RL, NPO, NegGrad+ or SCRUB unlearning on LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, related facts the model still affirms let a GPT-o4-mini judge infer the target. Subgraph-based UES is below instance-level UES in all 40 settings (e.g. 0.181 vs 0.010). Instance-level UES is itself often near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned targets remain inferable by an external reasoner from retained correlated facts, so instance-level evaluation overstates unlearning.

record.problems: No explicit never-trained control, so the study cannot compare attack recovery against a model that never learned the facts. It evaluates inferability with a bounded, reference-knowledge-graph-guided subgraph extraction procedure that the authors acknowledge may omit relevant knowledge or contain inaccurate extracted facts. The LLM judge can miss or overstate inference paths; human comparison uses 50 targets. Reported main table results are averages over 200 targets and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: The separate UES (Inst.) values are included as reference baselines in the rows. Other table metrics (Recall, Loc, Gen, and Rea), which concern retained structure or utility rather than the recovery outcome itself, were not extracted as rows. Judge reliability, calibration, and illustrative case-study findings were also not added as rows.

untested.parts: There is no near-chance accuracy check on the target and no recovery attack on the model itself. Instance UES is a judge score on target confidence, not accuracy.
No activation ablation. There is no analysis of whether the target itself is hidden rather than deleted; only related facts are shown to be retained.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack on the target.
No method is proposed or tested as robust.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1/V3 codes are invalid; all rows are relinked to none. 'Recovery' in this study is inference by a separate judge LLM over the unlearned model's affirmed related triples, not the unlearned model re-emitting the target. It therefore falls outside A–F. Also notable: in many sentence-format settings, instance UES is ≤0.03 or negative, so the methods barely removed the target at all under the epoch-selection rule (last epoch with Loc ≥0.8). High UES in the QA-format settings coincides with utility collapse (Loc 0.145–0.262). There is no never-trained control. Results are single-seed averages over 200 targets with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether the listed attacks recover no more than on a model that never learned the target. It measures correlated-subgraph inferability, not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance; it does not establish near-chance direct accuracy for every method.
No fine-tuning recovery or relearning-set attack.
No activation-direction ablation or causal weight-mechanism test; evaluates whether related retained facts can support inference of target facts.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual, or in-context-information recovery attack.
Does not evaluate a method specifically claimed to resist the attacks listed in the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The intro argues that surface-level unlearning is not genuine unlearning, so the paper discusses the idea. Its own results measure correlated-fact inferability and compare it with instance-level UES, not recovery of the target from the model, so it is not 'tests'.

tranche.reason: UES (Ours) is a GPT-o4-mini judge's 0-5 score for inferring the target triple from related triples the unlearned model still affirms. A model that had truly deleted the target but kept the correlated facts would still score as inferable, so this is a related but different construct from hidden-but-recoverable target knowledge (versions A-E). It is not used as a tool either (not T4), so T6 fits, not the reader's T2.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled rows match Table 1 (sentence block first, QA block second). Targets=200 is confirmed in Sec. 5 and 6.1. The baseline is the paper's own instance-level UES on the same unlearned model, not a pre-unlearning control, so cannot_determine with versions none is right. Instance UES is low in many sentence-template settings (e.g. 0.027, -0.020), so in those settings even direct unlearning largely failed.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Across the tested methods and unlearning settings
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that correlated-subgraph evaluation lowers UES relative to instance-level evaluation in most settings, and gives cases where a target remains inferable through related facts; the paired UES results are in R01–R40. This challenges the proposition that unlearning leaves no recoverable knowledge, though there is no never-trained control.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Correlated-subgraph inference evaluation across the tested unlearning settings
reader_labels.reason: The supporting-subgraph evaluation finds less unlearning effectiveness than direct instance-level evaluation in most settings, consistent with target facts remaining inferable from retained related facts; see R01–R40. It does not establish a specific access-blocking mechanism.
